voice_intro: This is LIRIL. You are entering a multi-hour documentary of the public record of Canada — the entire open history from nations before the Crown to this hour, built from government documents, commissions, statutes, Hansard, and public social posts by officials and named subjects. A complete playthrough takes many hours. Progress is saved. Pause freely.
title: LIRIL — The Full Record of Canada
subtitle: Entire history of Canada via open government records and public social evidence

chapters.title: The contract — primary sources only
chapters.narration: This is LIRIL. What you are about to watch is not opinion journalism and not a party broadcast. It is a documentary of the public record of Canada — assembled from open government documents, Hansard, Auditor General reports, Statistics Canada, court records, royal commissions, and public social-media posts by officials and named subjects. Every major claim will land on a source. Where the record is incomplete, we say so. Where a statement is inference, we label it. The film runs for hours because the country is not a soundbite.

chapters.title: How to watch a multi-hour public record
chapters.narration: You can watch continuously, pause, jump by era, or open any source in a new tab. Each beat holds government documents and public social posts long enough to read. WATCH mode advances automatically. NAVIGATE mode lets you scrub acts like chapters of a book. Progress is saved in this browser so a multi-hour film can be finished over days.

chapters.title: The arc — from foundation to this hour
chapters.narration: The film tracks Canadian state power from Indigenous nations and first contact, through conquest and Confederation, residential schools and the Indian Act, war and welfare-state construction, the Charter, free trade, the security state after two thousand one, and the multi-axis present: procurement failure, MAID expansion, housing collapse, foreign interference findings, media capture, and social amplification. The destination is not a conspiracy. It is a timeline of open records leading to today.

chapters.title: Open government + open social as one continuous feed
chapters.narration: Modern accountability requires both ledgers and timelines. Federal open data, Access to Information releases already published, committee testimony, and public posts by ministers, crown corporations, unions, and named citizens form one evidence graph. TENET5's local OSINT vault freezes public fetches with timestamps. Private messages and private persons are out of scope.

chapters.title: Turtle Island — nations before Confederation
chapters.narration: Long before Canada existed as a state, hundreds of Indigenous nations governed territory, law, trade, and diplomacy across the land. Any honest history of Canadian government power begins here — not as decoration, but as the first continuous legal and social order the later Crown would attempt to displace, absorb, and rewrite through statute and force.

chapters.title: Contact economies — fish, fur, flags
chapters.narration: European seasonal fisheries and fur trade posts transformed power without yet building a modern federal state. Competition among French, English, and later American interests turned Indigenous diplomacy into a strategic theatre. The pattern that returns later is already visible: resource extraction, imperial rivalry, and local alliances written down by outsiders.

chapters.title: New France — seigneury, missions, war
chapters.narration: Quebec, missions, the seigneurial system, and imperial war with Britain defined a colonial order that still shapes language politics and civil law. Indigenous nations were not spectators; they were military and commercial partners and adversaries. The state's later claim to a single sovereignty is built on top of this contested map.

chapters.title: The Conquest and the Royal Proclamation
chapters.narration: The fall of Quebec and the seventeen sixty-three Royal Proclamation are foundational legal events. The Proclamation recognized Indigenous title in large parts of the interior and set rules for Crown acquisition of land — a standard later governments would dilute, ignore, or litigate for centuries. This is not myth. It is statute and proclamation history.

chapters.title: British North America — Quebec Act to rebellions
chapters.narration: The Quebec Act, Loyalist migration, the War of eighteen twelve, and the rebellions of eighteen thirty-seven and thirty-eight forced constitutional redesign. Responsible government emerges as a demand against colonial oligarchy — the Family Compact and Château Clique. The film tracks a recurring Canadian theme: elites manage reform just enough to preserve the core of power.

chapters.title: Union, railways, and the pressure to federate
chapters.narration: Debt from canals and railways, American expansion anxiety, and deadlocked legislatures push elites toward a larger federal bargain. Confederation will be sold as necessity. The film will later ask whether the modern federal state still serves the public — or has become a capture surface.

chapters.title: Haudenosaunee Confederacy — Great Law of Peace
chapters.narration: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy's Great Law of Peace is among the oldest continuous constitutional traditions on this continent. Clan mothers, council fire, and treaty protocols predate the Canadian Crown. Any film about Canadian government power that skips this order is not a history of the land — only a history of the later state.

chapters.title: Anishinaabe, Cree, Dene, Inuit — plural sovereignty
chapters.narration: Anishinaabe, Cree, Dene, Mi'kmaq, Inuit and dozens of other nations held distinct legal orders, trade routes, and seasonal territories. Confederation did not create law on empty ground. It layered a new machine over living systems the Crown later tried to erase by statute.

chapters.title: Pacific and Plains polities — wealth, war, ceremony
chapters.narration: Pacific Northwest potlatch economies and Plains buffalo diplomacy were not 'pre-politics.' They were systems of wealth, honour, and alliance. When Canada later criminalized potlatch and starved Plains nations after the buffalo collapse, it was attacking competing sovereignties — a fact later admitted in federal reports and courts.

chapters.title: Cabot, Cartier, seasonal fisheries
chapters.narration: John Cabot's voyages and Jacques Cartier's expeditions enter the written European ledger. Seasonal Basque and Breton fisheries already used these waters. Contact begins as resource economics, not settlement myth. Primary voyages are archived; interpretation must stay bound to those texts.

chapters.title: Quebec founded — Champlain and alliances
chapters.narration: Samuel de Champlain founds Quebec in sixteen oh eight. French survival depends on Indigenous alliances and knowledge. The colony is thin, militarized, and missionary. This is the seed of a dual legal tradition that Canada still has not resolved cleanly.

chapters.title: Company of One Hundred Associates to royal colony
chapters.narration: Corporate charters fail; the Crown takes New France as a royal colony. Seigneurial tenure, Catholic missions, and military governance define social order. The pattern of state-corporate fusion — company first, Crown second — will reappear in railways, pipelines, and consulting contracts centuries later.

chapters.title: Great Peace of Montreal and the inland wars
chapters.narration: The Great Peace of Montreal and decades of inland war show Indigenous nations as diplomatic principals, not props. French, British, and Haudenosaunee strategy intertwine. Later Canadian schoolbooks compressed this into a simple conquest story. The primary treaties and council records are more complex.

chapters.title: Plains of Abraham — the Conquest
chapters.narration: Quebec falls. Montreal follows. The Conquest is not the end of French society — it is a transfer of imperial title that leaves a people, a language, and a civil law under a new sovereign. Every later language crisis sits on this military fact.

chapters.title: Royal Proclamation of 1763
chapters.narration: The Royal Proclamation recognizes Indigenous title across vast interior lands and restricts private purchase. It is still cited in Canadian courts. When modern governments treat land as already emptied of title, they fight their own foundational document.

chapters.title: Quebec Act — civil law and Catholic space
chapters.narration: The Quebec Act restores French civil law and expands Catholic practice under the Crown — strategic loyalty politics as American revolution gathers. It is a bargain: keep the colony by accommodating identity. Canadian federalism never escapes this bargain's aftershocks.

chapters.title: Loyalists and the Constitutional Act
chapters.narration: American independence drives Loyalist migration. Upper and Lower Canada are created in seventeen ninety-one. Settler politics, land grants, and oligarchic councils — Family Compact and Château Clique — set the template for elite capture that reformers will later name.

chapters.title: War of 1812 — border as identity forge
chapters.narration: The War of eighteen twelve is remembered differently in the United States and Canada. For British North America it becomes a founding myth of survival. Indigenous allies — including Tecumseh's confederacy — pay costs the later Canadian state will rarely centre in school narratives.

chapters.title: Rebellions — responsible government demanded
chapters.narration: Armed rebellion in Upper and Lower Canada forces London to send Lord Durham. Responsible government becomes the reform demand against colonial oligarchy. The pattern is familiar: crisis, commission, partial reform that preserves core power.

chapters.title: Durham Report — assimilation as policy
chapters.narration: Durham recommends uniting the Canadas and absorbing French Canadians into British institutions. Assimilation is not a side comment — it is explicit state strategy. Later residential schools and language fights sit in this intellectual lineage.

chapters.title: Act of Union and responsible government
chapters.narration: The Act of Union merges Upper and Lower Canada. Responsible government arrives mid-century. Cabinets answer to elected assemblies — but the franchise is narrow, women are excluded, Indigenous peoples are constrained, and property rules the vote. Democracy is partial by design.

chapters.title: Railways, debt, and the federal bargain
chapters.narration: Canal and railway debt, American expansion anxiety, and legislative deadlock push elites toward a larger federation. Confederation will be sold as necessity and destiny. The film later asks whether the modern federal machine still serves citizens — or only the intermediaries.

chapters.title: Charlottetown and Quebec Conferences
chapters.narration: Colonial politicians bargain federalism in closed conferences. The public is not co-author. Indigenous nations are not co-sovereigns at the table. The deal is elite, imperial, and strategic — a fact the primary conference records do not hide.

chapters.title: Confederation — a deal among elites
chapters.narration: The British North America Act creates the Dominion. Federal and provincial powers are divided. Indigenous nations are not parties at the table as equals. The new state inherits Crown claims and begins building national infrastructure with a political economy of patronage and land.

chapters.title: The Indian Act — statutory domination
chapters.narration: The Indian Act consolidates colonial control over status, band governance, land, and movement. It is not a side story. It is a central operating system of Canadian state power over Indigenous peoples — amended for generations, still in force, still litigated, still producing measurable harm.

chapters.title: Residential schools — policy as cultural destruction
chapters.narration: For more than a century, church-run and state-funded residential schools removed children from families. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission later documents cultural genocide. The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation holds the archive. This film will not soft-focus the statute trail or the body of survivor testimony.

chapters.title: Red River, numbered treaties, Northwest Resistance
chapters.narration: Expansion into the Northwest is not peaceful settlement mythology. Treaties, the Métis resistance, the hanging of Louis Riel, and the Canadian Pacific Railway bind the west into the Dominion under military and legal pressure. Land policy and railway capital co-author the map.

chapters.title: Chinese head tax and exclusion
chapters.narration: Racialized immigration law — head tax and later exclusion — builds a white dominion model while extracting labour for railways and cities. Later apologies do not erase the statutory record. The film treats immigration law as state design, not weather.

chapters.title: Total war, conscription, and state expansion
chapters.narration: World War One expands federal power: income tax, conscription crisis, wartime measures, and suppression of dissent. The modern administrative state learns muscle memory here — emergency powers first, permanent capacity later.

chapters.title: Depression — relief, revolt, and redesign
chapters.narration: Mass unemployment exposes the thinness of local relief. Bennett and King eras struggle with federalism and markets. The next war will unlock a welfare-state bargain Canadians are still living inside — and still arguing about who it excludes.

chapters.title: British North America Act in force
chapters.narration: July first, eighteen sixty-seven. The Dominion exists. Sections ninety-one and ninety-two divide powers. Residual federal power and peace, order, and good government clauses will later stretch into emergencies and criminal law. Read the text — not the fireworks.

chapters.title: Red River Resistance and Manitoba
chapters.narration: Métis assert rights as Canada purchases Rupert's Land. Louis Riel's provisional government forces negotiation. Manitoba enters Confederation with bilingual and denominational school guarantees later eroded. The state's first western expansion is already a legitimacy crisis.

chapters.title: Indian Act — the operating system
chapters.narration: The Indian Act consolidates control over status, band governance, land, and movement. It is still in force, still amended, still litigated. Residential schools, pass systems, and potlatch bans ride this statute. This is not ancient history — it is continuous administration.

chapters.title: Numbered Treaties — land for promises
chapters.narration: Numbered Treaties open the Prairies to settlement under Crown terms. Oral and written accounts diverge on what was promised. Modern courts, specific claims, and treaty commissions keep reopening the record. The film holds both the state text and the Indigenous legal memory.

chapters.title: Canadian Pacific Railway — nation and patronage
chapters.narration: The CPR is sold as national destiny and built with public subsidy, Chinese labour, and political scandal. Pacific Scandal topples Macdonald temporarily. Infrastructure and corruption travel together — a ledger the Auditor General will later keep for other megaprojects.

chapters.title: Northwest Resistance and Riel's hanging
chapters.narration: The eighteen eighty-five Northwest Resistance ends with military force and Riel's execution. Métis and Cree leaders face the state. The hanging deepens fracture lines still visible in western and Indigenous politics. Primary trial records and petitions remain the standard.

chapters.title: Residential schools — state policy of child removal
chapters.narration: Residential schools are not accidents of private charity. They are funded and regulated as state and church policy to break family and language. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission later documents cultural genocide. The film will return to those findings as legal anchors, not metaphors.

chapters.title: Laurier boom — immigration and exclusion
chapters.narration: Clifford Sifton's immigration machine fills the Prairies while Asian exclusion laws and head taxes show a racial hierarchy in statute. The Chinese head tax and continuous journey regulation are government instruments — not folk prejudice alone.

chapters.title: Great War — conscription and sacrifice
chapters.narration: Canada enters the First World War as a dominion and exits with national trauma, conscription crisis, and new industrial power. French-English splits harden. Veterans return to a state that will later fail many of them in housing and health — a pattern the modern Veterans Affairs record still documents.

chapters.title: Persons Case — women as legal persons
chapters.narration: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rules women are persons for Senate appointment. It is a constitutional milestone and a reminder that Canadian rights expansions often come from court fights, not elite generosity.

chapters.title: Depression — Bennett, relief camps, On-to-Ottawa
chapters.narration: Mass unemployment, relief camps, and the On-to-Ottawa Trek expose the thinness of federal social protection. Bennett's New Deal arrives late. Provincial and federal blame-shifting becomes a Canadian art form the film will see again in housing and health.

chapters.title: World War Two — total mobilization
chapters.narration: Conscription again, industrial mobilization, Japanese Canadian internment, and wartime bureaucracy reshape citizenship and rights. The internment is not a footnote — it is a primary case of emergency power against a racialized population on Canadian soil.

chapters.title: Post-war bargain — welfare state construction
chapters.narration: Family allowance, unemployment insurance expansion, public housing experiments, and the path to medicare build a social compact. Crown corporations and resource nationalism define an era when the state claims to secure life conditions — a claim the later film will test with modern metrics.

chapters.title: Cold War security culture
chapters.narration: Gouzenko, RCMP security service practices, and continental defence bind Canada into a security alliance culture. Oversight lags capability — a pattern that returns in CSIS eras and foreign interference inquiries decades later.

chapters.title: Quiet Revolution and national unity crisis
chapters.narration: Quebec's secular modernization, FLQ crisis, War Measures Act, and language laws force the federation to confront legitimacy. Trudeau-era federalism answers with rights language and central institutions — setting up the Charter bargain.

chapters.title: Patriation and the Charter of Rights
chapters.narration: Nineteen eighty-two patriates the constitution and entenches the Charter. Section thirty-five recognizes Aboriginal rights. Notwithstanding clause politics begin. Courts become a co-author of policy — including, decades later, the Carter decision that opens the MAID statutory path.

chapters.title: Free trade and continental integration
chapters.narration: FTA and NAFTA rewire economic sovereignty debates. Capital mobility rises; industrial policy fights shift. The later housing financialization and corporate concentration stories inherit this integration.

chapters.title: Oka, Ipperwash, and the unfinished land question
chapters.narration: Armed standoffs and deaths make land claims impossible to treat as closed history. Public inquiries follow. The film keeps land, policing, and Indigenous jurisdiction as live systems — not museum panels.

chapters.title: Second World War — mobilization and internment
chapters.narration: Canada mobilizes for total war. Japanese Canadian internment and property seizures are state policy later apologized for. The war also builds industrial capacity and expectations of full employment that seed the postwar welfare state.

chapters.title: Postwar welfare architecture
chapters.narration: Family allowances, unemployment insurance expansion, hospital insurance beginnings — the postwar settlement trades loyalty for security. Crown corporations and industrial policy expand. This is the high-water mark of state capacity the later neoliberal decades will erode while expanding coercive capacity elsewhere.

chapters.title: Points system — race-neutral on paper
chapters.narration: The points system retools immigration selection. Formally race-neutral criteria replace national-origin preferences. Outcomes still track global inequality and later temporary foreign worker expansions. The statute book is the evidence; political speeches are not.

chapters.title: Medicare — federal cost-share and values fight
chapters.narration: Federal medicare cost-sharing makes publicly funded physician care national. It is a rights and fiscal bargain. Later privatization pressures and MAID expansion will stress the same health system from opposite directions — both visible in Health Canada and provincial data.

chapters.title: October Crisis — War Measures Act
chapters.narration: The FLQ crisis triggers the War Measures Act. Civil liberties suspend in the name of order. The precedent of emergency power will be cited again in two thousand twenty-two under the Emergencies Act. Compare the statutes and the inquiries — do not rely on slogans.

chapters.title: Constitution Act 1982 and the Charter
chapters.narration: Patriation and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms transform litigation and politics. Section fifteen equality, section seven life liberty security, section one reasonable limits — the tools later MAID and public health cases will turn. Quebec does not sign. The constitutional wound remains.

chapters.title: Free trade — FTA to NAFTA
chapters.narration: Free trade elections realign Canadian politics. Economic integration with the United States deepens. Sovereignty debates become trade debates. Later digital and data sovereignty fights inherit this architecture.

chapters.title: Oka — land defence under cameras
chapters.narration: The Oka crisis puts Indigenous land defence on national television. It is not the first or last standoff. It forces a generation of Canadians to see that treaty and title disputes are present tense, not museum exhibits.

chapters.title: Somalia Affair — military scandal and reform
chapters.narration: The Somalia Affair forces public inquiry into Canadian Forces conduct and cover-up culture. Military justice and CFNIS later become permanent accountability files on this site. Scandals that do not produce structural change tend to recur.

chapters.title: Post-nine-eleven security expansion
chapters.narration: Anti-terrorism statutes, no-fly logic, and expanded intelligence powers arrive with continental pressure. Oversight and transparency do not expand at the same speed. The pattern: capability first, accountability later — if at all.

chapters.title: Sponsorship scandal — modern patronage on camera
chapters.narration: The Auditor General and Gomery inquiry expose advertising kickback networks after the referendum. Public trust in federal Liberals collapses. The scandal is a teaching case in procurement, parties, and the difference between audit findings and criminal closure.

chapters.title: Harper years — control, energy, and centralization of message
chapters.narration: Minority then majority Conservative government emphasizes fiscal messaging, resource development, and tight communications control. Accountability office fights and data controversies enter the public record. The film neither hagiographs nor demonizes — it tracks statutes, budgets, and audits.

chapters.title: Apology, TRC, and the unfinished implementation
chapters.narration: The residential school apology and TRC process produce Calls to Action. Implementation scorecards later show uneven progress. The film treats promises as measurable claims against open trackers.

chapters.title: Phoenix pay — the seed of a nine-billion failure
chapters.narration: A payroll transformation for the public service is planned under one government and detonates under the next. The Auditor General will later document a multi-billion remediation. Phoenix is the archetype of digital state failure that prefigures ArriveCAN-scale scandals.

chapters.title: Century Initiative and demographic planning assumptions
chapters.narration: A one-hundred-million population aspiration enters elite planning discourse. Immigration targets rise. Housing supply, healthcare capacity, and infrastructure lag. The film will later place targets against CMHC and Health Canada numbers — not slogans.

chapters.title: After September 11 — security state expansion
chapters.narration: Anti-terrorism statutes, no-fly lists, and intelligence budgets expand after two thousand one. Oversight lags. The security state and the welfare state reverse trajectories — more surveillance capacity, thinner social capacity. Primary statutes and SIRC/NSICOP reports are the evidence.

chapters.title: Sponsorship Scandal and Gomery
chapters.narration: The Sponsorship Scandal and Gomery Inquiry document Liberal Party of Canada era misuse of public funds for political ends. It is a textbook case of patronage networks. The public accounts and inquiry transcripts remain online.

chapters.title: Harper years — census, omnibus, Afghanistan
chapters.narration: Long-form census cancellation fights, omnibus bills, Afghanistan combat, and accountability office creation coexist. The film does not romanticize any party. It tracks instruments of power: how statutes, budgets, and appointments move regardless of brand colour.

chapters.title: 2015 mandate — sunny ways meet the machine
chapters.narration: A majority Liberal government promises transparency, reconciliation, and middle-class growth. The film scores promises against later ethics findings, AG reports, and statutory outcomes — not campaign video.

chapters.title: Carter and Bill C-14 — MAID enters statute
chapters.narration: The Supreme Court strikes the absolute ban on assistance in dying. Parliament enacts C-14. Health Canada annual reports will become the primary body-count ledger. This is the legal hinge for the later expansion arc tracked in Acts six through nine.

chapters.title: SNC-Lavalin — pressure on a Attorney General
chapters.narration: The ethics commissioner's report and committee drama document pressure regarding a deferred prosecution agreement. Resignations follow. The case is a primary ethics-process exhibit for modern PMO-minister relations.

chapters.title: MMIWG inquiry — genocide finding
chapters.narration: The National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls issues a genocide finding and calls for justice. Implementation remains a live accountability metric against federal and provincial responses.

chapters.title: Lobbying industrial complex — the always-on layer
chapters.narration: Registry data shows continuous pressure on health, finance, defence, and tech files. The film treats lobbying not as spice but as structural input to legislation — cross-linked to MAID, procurement, and foreign influence tracks.

chapters.title: TRC Final Report — cultural genocide finding
chapters.narration: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission documents residential schools as cultural genocide. Ninety-four Calls to Action become a public scoreboard governments still fail to complete on schedule. The finding is Canada's own commission speaking — not foreign propaganda.

chapters.title: Carter and Bill C-14 — MAID legalized
chapters.narration: Carter v Canada strikes down the absolute ban on assisted death. Bill C-14 creates medical assistance in dying under narrow conditions. Every later expansion starts from this hinge. Health Canada's annual reports will become the death ledger of the film.

chapters.title: MMIWG Inquiry — genocide finding
chapters.narration: The National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls finds genocide. Governments accept and then under-deliver. The film treats this as a second official genocide finding in four years — TRC and MMIWG — not as rhetoric.

chapters.title: Pandemic governance — emergency as operating system
chapters.narration: Public health orders, economic transfers, and procurement under emergency conditions redefine the citizen-state interface. ArriveCAN becomes the emblematic digital failure. The film holds AG findings and parliamentary scrutiny as the spine — not social media rumor.

chapters.title: ArriveCAN — cost overrun as case study
chapters.narration: A border app balloons far beyond initial estimates. GC Strategies and related contracting enter the public scandal lexicon. Auditor General work and committee testimony freeze the numbers. This is the digital-state failure lineage after Phoenix.

chapters.title: Freedom Convoy and the Emergencies Act
chapters.narration: Protest, occupation, and the first use of the Emergencies Act in its modern form produce a commission record and lasting polarization. Banking freezes and police powers become permanent political memory. Primary documents: proclamation, commission evidence, court challenges.

chapters.title: Bill C-7 — MAID expansion under pandemic parliament
chapters.narration: Eligibility expands beyond reasonably foreseeable death. Track two begins. Health Canada reports document rising counts. Disability advocates warn of structural coercion via poverty and care gaps — warnings the film preserves as contemporaneous dissent on the record.

chapters.title: Housing shock — rates, supply, and financialization
chapters.narration: Pandemic migration, low rates then hikes, investor demand, and chronic undersupply produce a generational affordability break. CMHC and Statistics Canada series are the primary instruments. Announced billions versus delivered units become a permanent gap chart on this site.

chapters.title: Pandemic powers and ArriveCAN
chapters.narration: Emergency orders, border apps, and procurement explode. ArriveCAN becomes the Auditor General's emblem of cost overrun. Phoenix pay already proved payroll failure; ArriveCAN proves app failure. Same pattern, different decade.

chapters.title: Bill C-7 — MAID expansion
chapters.narration: Bill C-7 expands MAID beyond reasonably foreseeable natural death and sets the track for mental illness alone. Disability advocates warn. Hansard and committee evidence preserve the warnings. The death counts that follow are Health Canada's numbers.

chapters.title: Emergencies Act — convoy and inquiry
chapters.narration: The federal Emergencies Act is invoked for the first time. Banks freeze. The Rouleau commission later rules the threshold met — a finding critics dispute. Primary order-in-council text, commission transcripts, and court challenges are the record. Social media of officials and organizers is public secondary evidence.

chapters.title: Foreign interference — Hogue and NSICOP
chapters.narration: Intelligence leaks, NSICOP reporting, and the Hogue Commission put PRC and other state interference into the public square. Diaspora intimidation and electoral integrity become permanent files. The film maps named processes without turning diaspora communities into suspects.

chapters.title: Media concentration and public subsidy stack
chapters.narration: Ownership concentration, Meta news blocks, and federal media supports reshape the information environment. CBC appropriations and Online News Act fights sit beside independent outlets. The five-generation warfare frame treats brand legitimacy as a strategic asset.

chapters.title: Defence procurement — CSC, ships, and capability lag
chapters.narration: Canadian Surface Combatant cost trajectories, recruitment crisis, and Arctic capability gaps enter AG and parliamentary scrutiny. The later Griffon GLLE pause is a continuation, not a novelty.

chapters.title: Opioid crisis — toxic supply and accountability
chapters.narration: Death counts mount under a toxic drug supply. Provincial experiments diverge. Federal-provincial blame cycles dominate. Public health data and coroner series are the primary instruments — not culture-war slogans alone.

chapters.title: Veterans and MAID offers — documented cases
chapters.narration: Parliamentary testimony and reporting document cases where veterans seeking assistance were directed toward MAID pathways. These are among the most severe legitimacy shocks in the modern social compact — preserved as primary case files on this site.

chapters.title: Carbon pricing politics and cost-of-living collision
chapters.narration: Federal carbon pricing becomes a central electoral and regional cleavage while inflation and housing stress peak. The film tracks statute and rebate design against public affordability metrics without collapsing into campaign ads.

chapters.title: Online harms bills — speech and platform power
chapters.narration: Successive online harms proposals raise questions about state power over digital speech, platform liability, and due process. Primary sources: bill texts, committee briefs, charter analyses — not only influencer panic.

chapters.title: Hogue Commission — foreign interference
chapters.narration: The Hogue Commission and NSICOP document foreign interference, naming the People's Republic of China as principal state actor and describing parliamentarians under foreign influence. Enforcement lags findings. That gap is the story.

chapters.title: Media funding and concentration
chapters.narration: Public funding of private media, CBC mandate fights, and ownership concentration reshape the information environment. Public social posts by broadcasters and influencers enter the OSINT graph. The film tracks money and amplification — not vibes.

chapters.title: Leadership transition and conflict-of-interest scrutiny
chapters.narration: Federal leadership change brings Brookfield and finance-network conflict questions into continuous public scrutiny. Ethics screens, asset structures, and procurement adjacency are tracked with primary documents — not vibes.

chapters.title: Griffon GLLE — eight-hundred-million-class pause
chapters.narration: Light helicopter replacement pause and pivot enter the live procurement cluster on the daily briefing. Capability timelines, industrial strategy, and Arctic readiness intersect. This is current ops, not history.

chapters.title: CBC / Northland Tales — public OSINT freeze
chapters.narration: Open sources freeze a taxpayer-adjacent prank production chain: Indigenous Screen Office listing of Counting Coup / NLT1, CBC Entertainment confirmation class, NPF letter on RCMP veterans, and social amplification across X. ATIP is optional depth — the public FACT base already stands.

chapters.title: Social media as official record — ministers, crowns, unions
chapters.narration: When institutions speak on X, Facebook, or YouTube, those posts become part of the open record. NPF inquiry demands, Legion support, opposition leader statements, and target exposures are timestamped evidence events — not noise. The film integrates them beside Hansard and AG PDFs.

chapters.title: MAID mental illness track — scheduled law
chapters.narration: Expansion to mental illness as sole condition has been delayed but remains a scheduled statutory horizon in public debate and prior legislative design. The film shows the document trail of delays and the Health Canada reporting spine — labeled as law-and-report, not prophecy.

chapters.title: The daily briefing — continuous film ending
chapters.narration: History does not stop at the last rendered chapter. The daily briefing is the forever epilogue: what Ottawa is doing this cycle, which procurement files moved, which metrics shifted, and which future-plan language appeared in primary documents. Return here after the film.

chapters.narration: Cabinets change. The open data portals, Hansard, Health Canada MAID reports, and lobbying registry keep publishing. Social platforms remain public records of officials' claims. TENET5 freezes those streams daily so the film can point to timestamps, not memory.

chapters.title: Lead-up complete — the present ledger
chapters.narration: You have now walked the open-record path from nations before the Crown to this hour. The remaining acts drill multi-axis present files: MAID totals, housing, procurement, defence, and citizen remedies. The history was not decoration. It is the control group that proves the pattern is structural.

chapters.title: Deep dive — MAID as statistical system
chapters.narration: Health Canada annual reports, provincial breakdowns, track-two patterns, and speech evidence form a multi-hour research surface of their own. This beat orients you into the MAID dossier cluster as a film-within-the-film.

chapters.title: Deep dive — money failures ledger
chapters.narration: Phoenix, ArriveCAN, sole-source consulting, and defence overruns compose a fiscal integrity documentary. Auditor General chapters are the narration. Public accounts are the score.

chapters.title: Deep dive — Article II evidence architecture
chapters.narration: The site's genocide-evidence architecture stacks TRC, MMIWG, coerced sterilization, fertility collapse, and MAID disability patterns under a legal-analytic frame. This beat is a map of that architecture — claims remain claim-leveled inside each dossier.

chapters.title: Deep dive — Section 504 citizen enforcement path
chapters.narration: When institutions fail to prosecute, Criminal Code section five-oh-four preserves a citizen path to lay an information. The film ends actionability with guides, not despair.

chapters.title: Deep dive — continuous OSINT operations
chapters.narration: Investigation threads, social graphs, lobbying scrapes, and Hansard corpora are living systems. The OSINT dashboard is the control room after the historical acts. Watch it like a continuing series.

chapters.title: What the continuous record demands
chapters.narration: If you watched from origins to this hour, you saw a state that learned to expand capacity faster than it expanded accountability. The remedy implied by the record is not a single election slogan. It is permanent public memory, continuous audit, and citizen tools that do not wait for permission.

chapters.title: Return daily — the film never ends
chapters.narration: Bookmark the daily briefing. Re-enter any act. Re-open any source. Share one primary document. This concludes the continuous cut of the LIRIL Canada film — until the next open record lands.
